extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students of humor studies; comedy writers and stand-up performers
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or analyzing humor that is framed around current events or issues that are important or popular at the current time, including forms (news parody, lists, cartoons) and the professional workflows used in stand-up comedy to create topical material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality (timeliness and relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor framed around a specific topic related to current events or dealing with issues that are important or popular at the current time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states the defining feature: topical humor is framed around a specific topic related to current events. Use current, widely discussed topics as material; the value of this humor often diminishes when the topic is no longer widely discussed in public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ephemeral value / shelf-life
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical humor often loses much of its pleasurable effect once the underlying event or public interest has ceased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud and the article note that topical jokes can be hugely effective at the moment but lose impact over time because they rely on shared, current knowledge—plan for short shelf-life or refresh material as events evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of topical humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical humor can take multiple forms beyond jokes: news parody, 'Top 10' lists, demotivators, cartoons, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the form that best fits the subject and audience; the page lists examples (news parody, 'Top 10' lists, demotivators, cartoons) and notes that older jokes can be repurposed into topical ones when salience changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to repurpose older jokes into topical ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Old jokes may be turned into topical ones due to newly acquired salience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor changing contexts and public discourse—an otherwise perennial joke can become topical if a new event or development makes its references relevant again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical perspective on news flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical jokes and news parodies emphasize the need to look critically at the flow of the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use topical humor not only to reference events but to critique and interrogate how news is presented and circulated, as noted by Liisi Laineste of the Estonian Literary Museum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalized idea harvesting (clippers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial stage: 'clippers' sift through numerous news headlines and lead paragraphs for joke ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic scanning of news sources and headlines is used to gather potential topics; this role emphasizes breadth of input and surface-level identification of funny material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke engineering (structure and pacing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'joke engineer' defines the structure of the joke: its components, the speed of its build-up, the idea of the punch line, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the internal architecture of the joke—component ordering, pacing, and where the punchline will land—before drafting wording. This is a planning/structuring role focused on mechanics of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke styling (draft creation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'joke stylist' creates a draft of the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate the engineered structure into actual language and phrasing, producing an initial version that can be reviewed and polished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polishing (the 'polish man')
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'polish man' refines the draft produced by the stylist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on tightening wording, sharpening punchlines, and improving clarity and impact. Polishing is iterative and aims to maximize the joke's immediate effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing coaching
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'timing coach' is responsible for the timing of phrases and pauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on delivery timing—phrases, pauses, and rhythm—to ensure the punchline lands. Timing is crucial for comedic effect and can be trained separately from content creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer delivery and personalization (talent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The performer ('talent') dry-runs the joke, adds personal individuality, and prepares 'recovery lines' for when a joke sizzles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery, persona, and contingency lines are essential: the same written material can succeed or fail depending on a performer's style, rehearsal, and ability to recover from a failed bit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recovery lines / contingency planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers prepare 'recovery lines' to use when a joke sizzles (fails).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate failures and have quick transitions or callbacks ready to maintain momentum; recovery planning is part of professional stand-up preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison with perennial jokes (durability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between jokes independent of topicality (perennial) and topical jokes that rely on contemporary allusions and lose impact when interest fades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating material, weigh whether to aim for immediate topical payoff or longer-term durability; Freud suggests perennial jokes are more reusable, while topical jokes may produce stronger immediate laughter but are context-dependent.
